verses.1: Al-Mizan reads al-ʿaṣr as an oath by time and, in light of the ensuing exception from loss for believers who adhere to truth and patience, most likely as the Prophet’s era, when Islam rose and truth vanquished falsehood. It records other readings: the afternoon, whose decline manifests divine power; the Afternoon Prayer, the middle and best obligatory prayer (2:238); day and night, called ʿaṣrān; time or history as a setting of signs of omnipotence; and, in some narrations, the Mahdi’s appearance, when truth will finally dominate falsehood. It says further interpretations exist.
verses.2: Al-Mizan takes al-insān to mean humankind generally and khusrin to mean loss of one’s capital or original asset; citing al-Rāghib, it notes that cognate terms describe loss suffered by a person or by an unsuccessful undertaking. The indefiniteness of khusrin either intensifies the loss or marks a loss unlike wealth or status: the loss of oneself and one’s family on Resurrection, “a manifest loss” (39:15).
verses.3: Al-Mizan holds that the verse qualifies humanity’s loss: faith and righteous deeds save people from it. Death transfers them to an eternal life; the tested life of this world determines future felicity or wretchedness because beliefs and deeds are manifested there as recompense (56:61), (13:26), (21:35), (53:39-41), (30:44), and (32:46). Life is capital invested for the hereafter: truth in belief and action yields blessed profit and safety, while falsehood and abandonment of faith and good works bring deprivation. Belief in God entails belief in all His messengers and the afterlife (4:150-151), and righteous deeds encompass every good act. The exception does not include believers who fall short of required righteous acts: loss is general, from the total loss of a deliberate atheist to the partial loss of a wicked believer temporarily in hell and later released through intercession or other means. Enjoining truth means counselling and steadfastness in true religion, and is wider than al-amr bil-maʿrūf wa al-nahy ʿan al-munkar because it includes belief and every encouragement to righteous action. It and enjoining patience are emphatic specifications within righteous deeds; the repeated verb confirms this. Their order after faith and deeds shows hearts opened to submission and concern that truth prevail and spread (39:22). Unqualified patience includes obedience, refraining from disobedience, and enduring afflictions decreed by God.
